why: Projects rarely fail on the Gantt chart alone: they fail when the wrong people are surprised, decisions wait for weeks and status reports hide the truth. Hiring managers for project managers test exactly this: how you map and engage stakeholders, report honestly, get decisions from a steering committee and close a project properly.
outcome: map stakeholders on a power/interest grid, build a RACI with one accountable per task, write a communication plan, produce an honest RAG status report, prepare a steering committee that takes decisions, run meetings and handle conflict, close a project with lessons learned, and explain PMP, PRINCE2 and CAPM.

lessons.title: Identifying stakeholders and the power/interest grid
text: A stakeholder is anyone who affects the project, is affected by it, or believes they are. The list is always longer than the org chart suggests: the sponsor and the business users, but also the IT security team that must approve the architecture, the works council (CSE in France) when jobs or working conditions change, the data protection officer when personal data is processed, the support team that will run the system, suppliers, and sometimes customers or regulators. Missing one early usually means a late veto.

Identify them in a workshop with the sponsor and key users, from the project charter, the org chart, the processes the project changes and similar past projects. Record each one in a stakeholder register: name and role, what they expect, what they fear, their influence, their current attitude and who in the team owns the relationship. The register is sensitive (it may say “resistant”), so keep it within the project management team.

The power/interest grid (often credited to Mendelow) places each stakeholder by power over the project (budget, veto, resources) and interest in it (how much it changes their work). High power, high interest: manage closely (involve them in decisions, meet regularly). High power, low interest: keep satisfied (short, rare, well-prepared updates; do not drown them in detail). Low power, high interest: keep informed (demos, newsletters, and listen: they often know the problems on the ground). Low power, low interest: monitor with minimal effort.

Positions move. A finance director with little interest becomes very interested the day the budget overruns; a team lead gains power when promoted. Review the grid at every phase. The PMBOK Guide also uses a stakeholder engagement assessment matrix: for each stakeholder, the current level (unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading) and the desired level. The gap shows where to spend your time: turning a resistant department head into a neutral one matters more than another meeting with a supporter.
points: Stakeholder: affects, is affected by, or believes they are affected by the project.
Stakeholder register: role, expectations, influence, attitude, relationship owner; keep it confidential.
Power/interest grid: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor.
Engagement levels: unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading; plan from current to desired.
Review the map at every phase: power and interest change.

example.code:
INTEREST
               low                  high
POWER  high | Keep satisfied     | Manage closely      |
            | CFO, CISO          | Sponsor, Ops VP     |
       low  | Monitor            | Keep informed       |
            | Facilities         | Call-centre agents  |
example.note: A CRM replacement: the CFO controls the budget but cares little until costs move; call-centre agents will use the tool every day but cannot stop the project.

lessons.title: RACI and project roles: sponsor, steering committee, project board
text: A RACI matrix lists the tasks or deliverables in rows and the people or roles in columns, with one letter per cell. R, Responsible: does the work. A, Accountable: owns the result, approves it and answers for it. C, Consulted: gives input before the work is done (two-way). I, Informed: is told of the result (one-way).

The rules interviewers check: exactly one A per row, because two accountable people means nobody is; at least one R per row (the A can also be the R on small tasks); few Cs, since every C slows the task down; a person with many As may be a bottleneck; a column with no R or A raises the question of whether that person needs to be on the project at all. Variants exist (RASCI adds S for support), but RACI is the one everyone recognises.

The sponsor owns the business case, secures the budget, chairs the steering committee and removes obstacles above the project manager’s level. The project manager plans, coordinates and reports, and is accountable for delivering within the agreed tolerances, not for the business benefits. The steering committee (COPIL in French companies) brings together the sponsor and senior managers of the departments concerned to take the decisions beyond the project manager’s authority: scope, budget, priorities, go / no-go.

In PRINCE2 the equivalent body is the project board, with three roles: the executive (one person, accountable for the project and its business case, the decision-maker), the senior user (represents those who will use the products and realise the benefits) and the senior supplier (represents those who design and build the products). The project manager runs the project day to day within the tolerances the board sets. French organisations often speak of MOA (maîtrise d’ouvrage, the business owner side) and MOE (maîtrise d’œuvre, the delivery side).
points: R does the work, A owns the result (exactly one), C gives input before, I is told after.
At least one R per task; few Cs; check people with too many As.
Sponsor: business case, budget, chairs the steering committee; PM: delivery within tolerances.
PRINCE2 project board: executive (decides), senior user, senior supplier.

example.code:
Task                     Sponsor  PM  Business lead  IT lead  DPO
Approve business case       A     R        C            C      I
Write requirements          I     A        R            C      C
Data protection review      I     R        A            C      C
Build and test              I     A        C            R      I
Go-live decision            A     R        C            C      I
example.note: One A per row. The PM prepares the sponsor’s decisions (R) and owns the project work (A); the DPO advises on data protection (C) while the business owner of the process remains accountable.

lessons.title: The communication plan: who, what, when, which channel
text: The communication plan answers, for each audience: what information they need, when, through which channel, from whom, and what feedback is expected. It comes from the stakeholder map: the steering committee gets a monthly decision pack, the core team a weekly meeting and a shared board, end users a newsletter and demos before go-live, the sponsor a short weekly call.

Communication channels grow quickly: between n people there are n × (n − 1) / 2 possible channels. Five people have 10, ten people have 45, twenty have 190. This is why large projects need a clear plan, single sources of truth (one project page, one RAID log, one decisions log) and named owners, rather than everybody copying everybody.

Choose the channel by purpose. Push (e-mail, newsletter, status report) for information people must receive; pull (project site, dashboard, wiki) for large audiences who look when they need to; interactive (meetings, calls, workshops) for anything that needs discussion, emotion or a decision. Bad news and changes that affect someone’s job are told face to face first, then confirmed in writing.

Adapt the message to the reader: an executive wants the decision needed, the impact and your recommendation in three lines; a developer wants the detail. Plan communication around key moments (kick-off, each go-live, a change of scope), and check that it works: do people come to the demos, are the same questions asked again, does the sponsor read the report?
points: Communication plan: audience, information, frequency, channel, owner, feedback.
Channels between n people: n × (n − 1) / 2; 10 people = 45.
Push, pull, interactive: decisions and bad news need interactive.
Executives: decision, impact and recommendation first.
Single sources of truth: project page, RAID log, decisions log.

example.code:
Audience            What                          When            Channel            Owner
Steering committee  Status, decisions needed      Monthly         Meeting + deck     PM (sponsor chairs)
Sponsor             Progress, risks, escalations  Weekly          30-min call        PM
Core team           Tasks, blockers, priorities   Weekly          Meeting + board    PM
End users           What changes, training dates  Monthly         Newsletter, demo   Business lead
Support team        Handover, known issues        Before go-live  Workshop           IT lead
example.note: Each line comes from the stakeholder map: the more power and interest, the more interactive the channel.

lessons.title: Status reports and RAG: reporting honestly
text: A status report tells, on one page, where the project stands against the plan and what is needed from the reader. A good structure: overall status with a one-line reason, achievements of the period, next steps, milestones (planned vs forecast), budget (spent, forecast at completion vs approved), top risks and issues with owners, and the decisions or help needed. Write it from the plan and the RAID log, not from memory.

RAG means red, amber, green. Define the thresholds in advance with the sponsor so the colours are not a mood: for example green when the forecast is within tolerance, amber when a tolerance is threatened but the team has a recovery plan, red when a tolerance will be exceeded without a decision from above. Many organisations use something like 5 % for amber and 10 % for red on cost or dates, but the thresholds are whatever the steering committee agreed.

A watermelon project is green outside and red inside: every report shows green until, a few weeks before the deadline, it turns red at once. It happens when amber is seen as a failure, when the project manager hopes to catch up quietly, or when reports measure activity (tasks done) instead of results (milestones met, tests passed). The cure: objective criteria, a culture where amber is welcomed as an early warning, and trends (the forecast date over the last weeks) rather than a single colour.

An amber or red status must come with the cause, the impact, the recovery plan and the decision needed. “Red: data migration” helps nobody; “Red: migration tests rejected 4 % of customer records; go-live on 15 May at risk by 2 weeks; recovery plan: 2 extra weeks of the data contractor for €9,600; decision needed: approve the cost or move go-live” lets the reader act.

Useful indicators: the percentage of milestones met on time, the forecast slip in days on the next key milestone, the budget forecast at completion against the approved budget (earned value is covered in the budget course), the number of open issues past their due date. One number with a trend says more than ten numbers without one.
points: One page: status, achievements, next steps, milestones, budget, risks and issues, decisions needed.
Agree the RAG thresholds with the sponsor before the first report.
Watermelon project: green outside, red inside; measure results, show trends.
Amber or red = cause, impact, recovery plan, decision needed.
Raise amber early: it is an early warning, not a failure.

example.code:
PROJECT ATLAS (CRM replacement)   Week 14   Overall: AMBER
Why amber: migration test rejected 4 % of records; go-live at risk by 2 weeks.
Done:      UAT cycle 1 complete (212 / 230 tests passed); training plan approved.
Next:      Fix mapping rules, migration test 2 (week 16), UAT cycle 2.
Milestone  Planned   Forecast  RAG
UAT end    10 Apr    17 Apr    A
Go-live    15 May    29 May    A
Budget     Approved 480k  Spent 301k  Forecast 492k (+2.5 %)  G
Top risk   Key users unavailable in May (owner: business lead)
Decision   Approve 2 extra weeks of the data contractor (EUR 9,600) by 18 Apr
example.note: The reader sees the colour, why, what is being done and what they must decide, in ten lines.

lessons.title: Steering committees: preparing decisions and escalating
text: The steering committee exists to take decisions, not to listen to a progress tour. Its members (the sponsor, heads of the departments concerned, often the IT director and a finance representative) meet monthly or at key milestones. A meeting where nothing is decided is a sign the agenda was wrong, or that the real decisions are taken elsewhere.

Prepare decisions before the meeting: send the pack two or three working days ahead, meet the key members one to one beforehand (pre-wiring) so nobody discovers a problem in the room, and present each decision with its options, their impact on time, cost, scope, quality and risk, and your recommendation. The committee chooses; your job is to make it easy to choose.

Escalation is normal, not a failure. In PRINCE2 terms, the project manager works within tolerances set by the project board and, when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, escalates with an exception report (manage by exception). Escalate early, with facts and options; escalate the problem, not the person; and tell the people concerned before they hear it in the committee.

A typical deck: 1) decisions needed (first slide, so they are taken even if time runs out), 2) overall status and RAG trend, 3) milestones and budget, 4) top risks and issues, 5) change requests, 6) next steps. After the meeting, send the minutes within 24 to 48 hours with decisions, actions, owners and dates, and update the decisions log.
points: The steering committee decides: scope, budget, priorities, go / no-go.
Send the pack 2 to 3 days ahead and pre-wire the key members.
Each decision: options, impacts, recommendation.
Manage by exception: escalate when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.
Decisions slide first; minutes within 48 hours.

example.code:
Steering committee #6 - 12 March
1. Decisions needed (2)
   D1 Move go-live 15 May -> 29 May (option A) or drop the reporting module (option B)
      Recommendation: A; cost +EUR 9,600, within budget tolerance
   D2 Approve change request CR-14 (new invoicing field): +6 days, +EUR 7,200
2. Status and RAG trend: G G A A
3. Milestones and budget
4. Top risks and issues
5. Change request log
6. Next steps and date of the next committee
example.note: Decisions come first, each with options, cost and a recommendation; the rest supports them.

lessons.title: Running meetings and handling conflict
text: Meetings are the most expensive tool of a project: eight people for one hour at an average loaded cost of €60 an hour is €480, and the same meeting every week for 46 working weeks is €22,080 a year. Every recurring meeting needs a purpose, only the people needed, and an agenda sent beforehand with the expected outcome of each item (inform, discuss, decide).

Run it well: start on time, recall the goal, timebox each item, park side topics in a “parking lot”, make sure the quiet people speak, and close by reading back the decisions and actions (who, what, by when). A decisions log records each decision with its date, who took it, the reason and the options rejected, so the same debate does not reopen three months later.

Conflict is normal in projects: priorities, resources, technical choices, personalities. The Thomas-Kilmann model names five modes: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating. Collaborating (solving the problem together) gives the most lasting result but takes time; competing can be right in an emergency; avoiding only buys time. The PMBOK Guide uses similar names: withdraw / avoid, smooth / accommodate, compromise / reconcile, force / direct, collaborate / problem solve.

For a difficult conversation (a stakeholder who blocks, a team member who misses deadlines, a sponsor who wants the impossible): prepare facts, not opinions; talk in private; describe the situation, the behaviour and its impact (the SBI model); listen to their side, there is often a constraint you did not know about; agree a concrete next step and confirm it in writing.

Teams go through stages (Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning); some conflict during storming is a sign the team is starting to work together, not that it is failing. Remote and hybrid meetings need extra care: everyone joins with the same tool, the chat is read, and decisions are written in the shared notes during the meeting.
points: Agenda with the expected outcome of each item; only the people needed.
Close by reading back decisions and actions: who, what, by when.
Decisions log: date, decision, who, why, options rejected.
Conflict modes: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating.
Difficult conversation: facts, in private, situation-behaviour-impact, listen, next step.

example.note: B1 attendees (8), B2 duration in hours (1), B3 average hourly cost (60), B4 meetings a year (46): B5 = 480 per meeting, B6 = 22,080 a year.

lessons.title: Closing a project: acceptance, handover, lessons learned
text: A project ends when its deliverables are accepted and handed over and its resources are released, not when the last task is ticked. A bad closure leaves an invisible cost: a system without an owner, contracts still running, a team that moves on without telling anyone what it learned.

Acceptance: the business owner signs off the deliverables against the acceptance criteria agreed at the start (user acceptance tests passed, open defects below an agreed level, documentation delivered). Record any reservations with an owner and a date. Without formal acceptance the project never ends: every new request becomes “part of the project”.

Handover to operations: the support and run teams receive the documentation, the runbooks, the list of known issues, access and monitoring, and the support model (who handles what, service levels). A hypercare period of a few weeks after go-live, during which the project team stays available, smooths the transition. Then close the administration: final costs against budget, supplier contracts ended or transferred, access removed, archives stored.

Lessons learned: hold a session with the team and key stakeholders, ideally from notes collected throughout the project, not only at the end. Ask what went well, what did not, and what we would do differently; turn each lesson into a recommendation someone can apply, and store it where the next project will find it. PRINCE2 makes “learn from experience” one of its principles: a new project starts by reading the lessons of previous ones.

The benefits often appear after the project ends: the business owner measures those of the business case (fewer calls, faster invoicing) later, following a benefits review plan. Finally, celebrate and thank people by name, including the business users and the support team; it closes the project for everyone and makes them willing to work with you again.
points: Formal acceptance against the agreed criteria; reservations with an owner and a date.
Handover: documentation, runbooks, known issues, support model, hypercare.
Administrative closure: final costs, contracts, access, archives.
Lessons learned: concrete recommendations stored for the next project.
Benefits measured after closure; celebrate and thank people by name.

example.code:
Closure checklist - Project Atlas
[x] Acceptance certificate signed by the business owner (2 reservations, owners named)
[x] Handover workshop with support; runbooks and known-issues list delivered
[x] Hypercare: 4 weeks, ended 26 June
[ ] Supplier contract closed, final invoice checked
[ ] Final cost report: 492k vs 480k approved (+2.5 %)
[ ] Lessons learned session (team + business), report stored in the PMO library
[ ] Benefits review planned with the business owner in 6 months
[ ] Team thanked, people released to their managers
example.note: Closure is a checklist with owners, not a farewell e-mail.

lessons.title: Certifications in short: PMP, PRINCE2, CAPM
text: PMP (Project Management Professional) is awarded by PMI, the Project Management Institute, a US-based association with members worldwide. It is the most widely recognised project management certification internationally. Candidates need experience leading projects (36 months with a four-year degree, 60 months without one) and 35 hours of project management education, then pass an exam that covers predictive, agile and hybrid approaches. It is renewed every three years with 60 professional development units (PDUs).

The PMBOK Guide (A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge), published by PMI, is its reference text. The current one is the 8th edition (November 2025). It keeps the principle-based approach of the 7th edition (2021) but makes it more practical: 6 principles (a holistic view, focus on value, embedded quality, accountable leadership, sustainability, empowered teams), 7 performance domains (governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources, risk), and process guidance brought back as non-prescriptive focus areas, with more on AI, PMOs and procurement. Many companies and courses still use the 7th edition’s 12 principles and 8 domains. The exam follows PMI’s exam content outline rather than one edition of the guide, so check the current outline before you study.

CAPM (Certified Associate in Project Management), also from PMI, is the entry-level certification: no project experience is required, only 23 hours of project management education. It suits graduates and career changers who want to show they know the vocabulary and the methods before they can apply for the PMP.

PRINCE2 (PRojects IN Controlled Environments) is a structured method that comes from the UK government, now owned by PeopleCert, which acquired AXELOS in 2021. The current version, PRINCE2 7 (2023), has 7 principles (continued business justification, learn from experience, defined roles, responsibilities and relationships, manage by stages, manage by exception, focus on products, tailor to suit the project), 7 practices, called themes in earlier versions (business case, organizing, plans, quality, risk, issues, progress), and 7 processes (starting up, directing, initiating a project, controlling a stage, managing product delivery, managing a stage boundary, closing a project). Its two main levels are Foundation (knowing the method) and Practitioner (applying it).

Which one in France and Europe? The PMP is a safe choice for international groups, consulting and IT services firms, and job offers that name it, but it needs experience first. PRINCE2 is very present in the UK, in the public sector and in some international organisations, and its Foundation level is quick to obtain. A junior profile can start with CAPM or PRINCE2 Foundation; software projects often also ask for an agile certification. In every case, interviewers care more about how you applied the ideas than about the badge.
points: PMP: PMI; 36 months of experience with a degree (60 without) + 35 hours of training; renewed every 3 years with 60 PDUs.
PMBOK Guide 8th edition (2025): 6 principles, 7 performance domains and focus areas.
CAPM: PMI entry level, no experience, 23 hours of training.
PRINCE2 7: 7 principles, 7 practices (formerly themes), 7 processes; Foundation then Practitioner.
Show how you applied the method: it counts more than the certificate.

PMP                    PRINCE2                   CAPM
Owner        PMI                    PeopleCert (AXELOS)       PMI
What         Certifies a person     Method; Foundation and    Entry-level
             (experience + exam)    Practitioner exams        certification
Experience   36-60 months leading   None for Foundation       None
             projects
Training     35 hours               Course usually taken      23 hours
Core ideas   Principles, domains,   Principles, practices,    PMI vocabulary
             predictive + agile     processes, stages         and basics
example.note: PMP certifies the person’s experience and knowledge; PRINCE2 is a method you learn and apply.

items: Role, expectations, influence, attitude, relationship owner
Manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor
High power, low interest: short, rare, prepared updates
Low power, high interest: demos, newsletters, listening
Owns and approves the result: exactly one per task
Owns the business case and budget, chairs the steering committee
PRINCE2: executive, senior user, senior supplier
PRINCE2: the single decision-maker, accountable for the business case
Number of communication channels between n people

Date, decision, who, why, options rejected

PMI: experience + 35 hours of training, 60 PDUs every 3 years
PMI entry level: 23 hours of training, no experience
6 principles, 7 performance domains and focus areas (2025)

pitfalls: Mapping stakeholders once at kick-off and never again.
Two accountable people on one task, or a RACI where everyone is consulted.
Reporting green until the last month (a watermelon project) instead of raising amber early.
A steering committee deck that tours progress and asks for no decision.
Surprising people in the committee instead of pre-wiring the ones concerned.
Meetings without an agenda, decisions or written actions.
Closing without formal acceptance or handover, so the project never really ends.

exercises.q: Excel: in G2, count the stakeholders whose power is E2 and whose interest is F2 (here High / High: the ones to manage closely).
exercises.hint: COUNTIFS takes pairs: a range, then its condition. Point at E2 and F2 rather than typing "High".
exercises.explain: COUNTIFS(B2:B9,E2,C2:C9,F2) counts the rows where both conditions hold: Sponsor, Operations director and Works council, so 3. Change E2 to High and F2 to Low and the same formula counts the stakeholders to keep satisfied (2).

exercises.q: Excel: a RACI must have exactly one A per task. In G4, return "OK" when row 4 has exactly one A, otherwise "Fix".
exercises.hint: COUNTIF(B4:F4,"A") counts the A letters of the row; compare it with 1 inside IF.
exercises.explain: COUNTIF(B4:F4,"A") gives 2 for the go-live decision (sponsor and PM), so the formula returns Fix: the PM should be R (prepares the decision) and the sponsor the only A. Copied down the column, it checks every task.

exercises.q: Excel: column B holds each milestone’s delay in days (0 or negative = on time). In D2, compute the share of milestones delivered on time (a fraction, e.g. 0.5 for 50 %).
exercises.hint: COUNTIF with the condition "<=0" counts the milestones on time; divide by the number of milestones.
exercises.explain: Three milestones out of six have a delay of 0 or less (Charter, Design, UAT): 3 / 6 = 0.5, so 50 % on time. Format the cell as a percentage; COUNTA(A2:A7) works as the denominator too.

exercises.q: Excel: in B6, compute the annual cost of this weekly meeting: attendees × duration × average hourly cost × meetings per year.
exercises.hint: Multiply the four cells B2 to B5.
exercises.explain: 8 × 1.5 × 65 = 780 per meeting, × 46 = 35,880 a year. Cutting it to 45 minutes with 6 people saves more than half: a strong argument for a smaller, shorter meeting.

exercises.q: Match each position on the power/interest grid with the right strategy.
exercises.answer: Involve the powerful and interested in decisions, give short prepared updates to the powerful but less interested, keep the interested informed and listen to them, and watch the rest in case their position changes.

exercises.q: Sort these items: what belongs in a one-page status report, and what does not?

groups.name: Belongs in the status report
items: Overall RAG with a one-line reason
Top risks and issues with owners
Budget: spent and forecast at completion

groups.name: Does not belong
items: Who is to blame for the delay

exercises.answer: The report helps the reader understand the situation and act: status, milestones, budget, risks and decisions. Task lists and logs stay in the tools, blame and opinions stay out.

exercises.q: Put the closing steps of a project in order.
steps: User acceptance tests passed against the agreed criteria
Formal sign-off by the business owner
Final cost report and supplier contracts closed
Lessons learned report stored for future projects
Team thanked, released and the success celebrated
exercises.answer: Prove the criteria are met, get the sign-off, hand over to the people who will run it, close the administration, record what was learned, then release and thank the team.

exercises.q: Your project is amber: a supplier delay threatens go-live by three weeks, and you have a recovery plan. Two days before the steering committee, the sponsor asks you to show green “to avoid alarming the board”.

choices.label: Explain privately why it is amber under the agreed thresholds, and what the board will need to decide
choices.feedback: You keep the report honest and show the sponsor that amber with a plan is a sign of control, not of failure.

choices.label: Show green as asked: the sponsor is your boss
choices.feedback: This is how watermelon projects are born: when the delay becomes visible, the board loses trust in you and in the sponsor.

choices.label: Show red to be covered whatever happens
choices.feedback: Overstating the problem is also dishonest, and it causes panic and decisions nobody needs.

steps.text: The sponsor is still worried about how it will look. Next?

choices.label: Present amber with the cause, the recovery plan and a clear decision request, and offer the sponsor to present the recovery plan
choices.feedback: The sponsor appears in control, and the board can decide with the facts.

choices.label: Keep amber in the deck but skip it when presenting
choices.feedback: A hidden amber is still a watermelon: the board needs to hear it and decide.

steps.text: After the committee approves the recovery plan?

choices.label: Send the minutes with the decision within 48 hours and track the recovery weekly with the sponsor
choices.feedback: The decision is recorded, and the next report shows whether the plan works.

choices.label: Wait for next month’s committee to report on it
choices.feedback: A month without follow-up can turn amber into red without anyone noticing.

exercises.answer: Report the status the agreed thresholds give, with the cause, the recovery plan and the decision needed. Help the sponsor look in control rather than hiding the problem, record the decision and follow the recovery closely.

exercises.q: Which RACI row is valid? (columns: Sponsor, PM, Business lead, IT lead)
exercises.answer: Exactly one A and at least one R: “A, R, C, I”. Two As means nobody really owns the result; a row without A or R has no owner or nobody doing the work.

exercises.q: Which statement about PRINCE2 and PMP is correct?
options: PRINCE2 is a PMI certification based on the PMBOK Guide
PMP is a method with seven processes, starting with “Starting up a project”
PRINCE2 is a method with principles, practices and processes; PMP certifies a person’s experience and knowledge of PMI’s standards
Both require five years of project experience before the first exam
exercises.answer: PRINCE2 (PeopleCert, formerly AXELOS) is a method with 7 principles, 7 practices and 7 processes; its Foundation exam needs no experience. PMP (PMI) certifies a person with experience and training requirements.

exercises.q: A project team has 10 people who all need to communicate with each other. How many communication channels are there?
exercises.answer: n × (n − 1) / 2 = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45. Adding just 5 people makes 105: a reason for a communication plan and single sources of truth.

exercises.q: Write a one-page status report for this situation: CRM replacement, week 20. Budget approved 480k, spent 350k, forecast at completion 505k. UAT: 90 % of tests passed. Go-live planned on 15 June, now forecast on 29 June because a supplier’s billing interface is two weeks late. Top risk: trainers not available in June. Agreed thresholds: amber above 5 % or up to 2 weeks late, red above 10 % or more than 2 weeks.
exercises.answer: PROJECT ATLAS, week 20. Overall: AMBER (go-live forecast 2 weeks late, budget forecast +5.2 %, both within the red thresholds). Why: the supplier’s billing interface is delivered 2 weeks late. Done: UAT cycle 2, 90 % of tests passed; the remaining failures are logged with owners. Next: integrate and test the billing interface (weeks 21-23), final UAT, go-live rehearsal. Milestones: UAT end planned 1 June, forecast 15 June (A); go-live planned 15 June, forecast 29 June (A). Budget: approved 480k, spent 350k, forecast 505k (+25k, +5.2 %) (A); the extra cost is the longer contractor period. Top risks: trainers not available in June (owner: business lead; mitigation: book trainers for July or train key users as trainers); supplier slips again (owner: PM; weekly supplier checkpoint, penalty clause reviewed). Decisions needed by the next committee: approve the new go-live date of 29 June and the 25k overrun, or keep 15 June without the billing interface and a manual workaround. Recommendation: move to 29 June.

interview.q: How do you identify and prioritise stakeholders on a new project?
interview.a: I start from the charter and the processes the project changes, then run a workshop with the sponsor and key users to list everyone who affects or is affected by it, including support, security, data protection and works council. I record them in a register and place them on a power/interest grid: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor. I compare their current and desired engagement and spend my time where the gap is biggest, and I review the map at each phase.

interview.q: Your project is behind schedule. How do you report it?
interview.a: Early and with facts. I apply the RAG thresholds agreed with the sponsor, so if the forecast passes a tolerance it is amber or red whatever my hopes. I give the cause, the impact on dates and cost, the recovery options and my recommendation, and I tell the sponsor before the committee. Hiding it creates a watermelon project, and then nobody trusts any report.

interview.q: A senior stakeholder keeps resisting the project. What do you do?
interview.a: I meet them one to one to understand why: often a fear of losing control, extra workload or a past bad experience. I check whether the concern is valid and can be addressed in scope, planning or training, and involve them where their expertise helps. If the resistance blocks decisions, I agree with the sponsor how to handle it, and escalate the issue, not the person, to the steering committee with options.

interview.q: How do you prepare a steering committee?
interview.a: I start from the decisions needed. I send the pack two or three days ahead with decisions on the first slide, each with options, impacts and my recommendation, then status, milestones, budget, risks and change requests. I pre-wire the key members so nobody is surprised. After the meeting I send the minutes within 48 hours with decisions, actions, owners and dates, and update the decisions log.

interview.q: What is a RACI, and which mistakes do you look for?
interview.a: A matrix of tasks and people saying who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed. I check that each task has exactly one A and at least one R, that there are not too many Cs slowing things down, that one person is not A for everything, and that everyone on the matrix has a real role. I validate it with the people named, not alone.

interview.q: How do you close a project?
interview.a: Formal acceptance against the agreed criteria, with reservations tracked; handover to operations with documentation, runbooks, known issues and a support model, then a hypercare period; administrative closure of contracts, costs and access; a lessons learned session that produces recommendations stored for the next projects; a benefits review planned with the business owner; and thanking the team and the business users.

interview.q: PMP or PRINCE2: which would you choose, and why?
interview.a: It depends on the context. PMP, from PMI, certifies experience and knowledge across predictive, agile and hybrid approaches and is widely recognised internationally, so it fits consulting and international groups, but it requires several years of project leadership. PRINCE2 is a structured method with principles, practices and processes, common in the UK and the public sector, and its Foundation level is quick. What matters most is showing how I applied the ideas: business justification, stages, tolerances, stakeholder engagement.

interview.q: Tell me about a conflict in your team and how you handled it.
interview.a: With the STAR structure: the situation (two leads disagreeing on the priority of a data migration versus new features), my task (a decision before the sprint), the actions (meeting each one in private to hear their constraints, then a joint session with the facts on risk and dates, a collaborative option that phased the work, and the decision written in the decisions log) and the result (the migration done on time, and both leads agreeing on how to settle future priority conflicts).
